reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Intermittent claudication is exertional muscle pain relieved by rest, with the site of pain located one level below the culprit arterial segment
Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia is defined by rest pain, non-healing ulceration, or gangrene and represents the severe end of the disease spectrum
An ankle-brachial index below the normal range supports the diagnosis, while calcified incompressible vessels can spuriously elevate readings, making toe pressures useful
Examination may reveal diminished pulses, cool skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, and delayed capillary refill
Duplex ultrasound and CT or MR angiography map disease and guide revascularisation planning
Structured exercise therapy, smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy, and statin use are cornerstones of management for claudication
Revascularisation, whether endovascular or open bypass, is reserved for lifestyle-limiting claudication that fails medical therapy or for limb-threatening ischaemia
Peripheral arterial disease is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis, so cardiovascular risk reduction is as important as limb-directed treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic limb ischaemia results from progressive atherosclerotic narrowing of the aortoiliac, femoropopliteal, or tibial arteries, reducing perfusion to the lower limb. In claudication, resting flow is adequate but cannot meet the increased metabolic demand of exercising muscle, producing reversible ischaemic pain. As stenoses progress and collateral capacity is exceeded, resting perfusion falls below tissue requirements, causing rest pain, ulceration, and tissue loss. Diabetes and renal disease accelerate distal and calcified disease, and the combination of impaired inflow and microvascular dysfunction underlies poor wound healing.
additionalDifferentials: Venous claudication from chronic venous obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Ankle-brachial index and toe pressures, with exercise testing when resting indices are equivocal
Arterial duplex ultrasound to localise stenoses and occlusions
CT or MR angiography, or catheter angiography, for revascularisation planning
Assessment of cardiovascular risk factors including lipids, glucose, and renal function
Wound assessment and, where infection or osteomyelitis is suspected, appropriate imaging
redFlags: Rest pain, non-healing ulcer, or gangrene indicating chronic limb-threatening ischaemia requiring urgent vascular referral
Rapidly progressing tissue loss or spreading infection threatening limb viability
Sudden worsening suggesting acute-on-chronic thrombosis or embolism, a limb-threatening emergency
Systemic sepsis arising from an ischaemic infected foot
reference.prognosis: Most patients with claudication remain stable and only a minority progress to limb-threatening ischaemia, but overall mortality is high because of concurrent coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia carries a substantial risk of amputation and death without timely revascularisation and wound care.
pitfalls: Interpreting a normal ankle-brachial index as excluding disease when vessels are calcified and incompressible
Attributing all leg pain to arterial disease and missing neurogenic or musculoskeletal causes
Focusing on the limb while neglecting the high systemic cardiovascular risk
Delaying referral in limb-threatening ischaemia, allowing avoidable tissue loss
management: Cardiovascular risk reduction with smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy and statin treatment as the foundation of care
Supervised structured exercise therapy for intermittent claudication
Optimisation of diabetes and hypertension, with cilostazol considered to improve claudication symptoms
Revascularisation by endovascular angioplasty and stenting or by surgical bypass for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia or lifestyle-limiting claudication
Wound care, offloading and treatment of infection or osteomyelitis in tissue loss, with meticulous foot protection
Urgent revascularisation assessment for rest pain, non-healing ulceration or gangrene, reserving amputation for the unreconstructable or non-viable limb
Surveillance of graft and stent patency alongside ongoing cardiovascular follow-up
